edits.why: Register the isotretinoin intracranial hypertension source question on this brief.

edits.old: Papilledema → MRI (venography if otherwise normal ⚠︎), then LP with an opening pressure → idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
edits.new: Papilledema → MRI to exclude mass or hydrocephalus, with MR venography to exclude venous sinus thrombosis, then LP with an opening pressure → idiopathic intracranial hypertension; ask first about retinoids, tetracyclines, vitamin A and growth hormone.
edits.why: MR venography is in the source, so the warning flag is removed; adds the drug history to the papilledema exit ramp.

edits.anchor: Simple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans/combination analgesics on ≥10 days/month ⚠︎
edits.text: Exit / pressure branchDrug-induced or idiopathic intracranial hypertension: stop the offending drug (isotretinoin, tetracyclines, vitamin A, growth hormone), which usually resolves it; acetazolamide, or topiramate as an alternative; weight loss if overweight, including bariatric surgery in adultsVision worsens despite medical therapy: urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting
edits.why: The brief had no treatment for the pressure branch; source treatment list added as an exit row matching the ladder columns.

edits.old: High opening pressure after a normal MRI
edits.new: High opening pressure (over 250 mm H2O) with normal CSF composition, after normal MRI and MR venography
edits.why: Adds the source cutoff and the normal-CSF requirement, and places LP after both imaging studies.

edits.text: Visual fields and acuity, for papilledemaSupportsEnlarged blind spots, otherwise full fieldsRaised pressure; a bitemporal defect instead points to a chiasmal lesion Medication and weight history, for papilledemaCauseRetinoid, tetracycline, vitamin A or growth hormone; recent weight gainSecondary intracranial hypertension; stop the drug MR venography, for papilledemaNextNo venous sinus thrombosisRequired before calling it idiopathic or drug-induced; done with the MRI, before LP
edits.why: Workup order for papilledema: fields, drug history, MRI with MRV, then LP.

edits.text: Papilledema on a drug: the tell and the mimics Bilateral disc edema, decreased acuity, full fields, normal neurologic examination, on isotretinoin — medication-induced intracranial hypertension; daily morning headache with nausea and vomiting, brief visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia from a CN VI palsy, and headache worse lying flat are the pressure features · Mechanism — impaired CSF resorption and venous hypertension; risk rises with obesity, recent weight gain and female sex after puberty · Optic chiasm glioma — compression of the chiasm gives a bitemporal field defect; full fields exclude it · Optic neuritis — acute painful vision loss, pain with eye movement, usually one eye; no morning headache or vomiting · Cluster headache — unilateral periorbital attacks with autonomic signs, typically adult men; never papilledema · Viral encephalitis — fever and altered mental status, both absent
edits.why: Teaches the deciding findings of the source question and maps each original distractor to why it fails; no such block existed.

edits.old: the pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does.
edits.new: the pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does. Fat-Soluble Vitamin Deficiency and Toxicity covers vitamin A excess, the same pressure mechanism as the retinoid that caused papilledema in the isotretinoin question.
edits.why: Cross-links the retinoid and vitamin A cause of intracranial hypertension.

notes: No contradiction with the source. Removed the warning flag on MR venography in the papilledema exit ramp because the source supports it. Added the LP cutoff over 250 mm H2O from the source; the pediatric criteria's higher cutoff was left out as specialist detail. Pairs-with sentence names Fat-Soluble Vitamin Deficiency and Toxicity (vitamin A).
